extracted.intended_audience: OSHA-regulated employers, workplace safety and health professionals, state-plan agencies, and stakeholders (employers, employer representatives, labor organizations)
extracted.subtask_short: heat injury and illness prevention standard
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed OSHA regulatory requirements and implementing provisions for a Heat Injury and Illness Prevention (HIIPP) standard, including training, measurement and recordkeeping, break requirements, program documentation, effective/compliance dates, and cross-application to multiple OSHA parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training — supplemental/refresher triggers and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers would be required to conduct refresher trainings annually for both at-risk workers and designated persons. Supplemental trainings would also be required for at-risk workers when (1) worker(s) heat exposure changes, (2) policies and procedures change, (3) worker(s) does not retain information, or (4) a heat-related injury or illness occurs at the work site that results in death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explicitly lists the four triggers for supplemental training and requires annual refreshers; the document also notes supplemental trainings intended to avoid double-counting when accounting for if-needed rest breaks for new/returning employees. Employers should plan training schedules to meet both annual and trigger-based supplemental requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training presentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Training must be provided in a language and at a literacy level each employee, supervisor, and heat safety coordinator understands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The employer must provide employees with an opportunity for questions and answers about the training materials. OSHA expects to provide training materials and templates and states that employers who incorporate OSHA materials may need less time to develop training. (OSHA welcomes comment on training development time assumptions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site indoor measurements requirement and recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: If the employer conducts on-site measurements at indoor work areas pursuant to paragraph (d)(3)(ii) of this section, they must have written or electronic records of those indoor work area measurements and retain those records for 6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record retention requirement is six months for indoor work-area measurements made under the cited measurement paragraph. The rule cross-references paragraph (d)(3)(ii) for when such measurements are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements implemented at no cost to employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The implementation of all requirements of this standard must be at no cost to employees, including paying employees their normal rate of pay when compliance requires employee time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA states this explicitly to make clear both material costs and employee time spent complying (e.g., training, breaks) must not reduce employee pay or impose costs on employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: This standard is effective [60 days after date of publication of the final rule in the Federal Register].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effective date is stated as 60 days after final-publication in the Federal Register; this is the date the rule becomes legally effective (distinct from compliance date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must comply with all requirements of this standard by [150 days after date of publication of the final rule in the Federal Register].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The compliance date (150 days after publication) is the deadline by which covered employers must have implemented the standard's requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each provision within this standard is separate and severable from the other provisions. If any provision is held to be invalid or unenforceable, that provision shall be construed to give it maximum lawful effect or, if utterly invalid, severed from the standard without affecting the remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard legal severability clause included to preserve remainder of the rule if any provision is invalidated; used for statutory/regulatory resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-application to other OSHA parts (identical requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements applicable to shipyard employment (29 CFR 1915.95), marine terminals (29 CFR 1917.32), longshoring (29 CFR 1918.148), construction (29 CFR 1926.67), and certain agricultural operations (amendment to 29 CFR 1928.21) are identical to the requirements set forth at 29 CFR 1910.148.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA adds sections in multiple parts stating the heat injury and illness prevention requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.148, thereby extending the same substantive duties across several industry-specific parts; several specific part/section citations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to have a written HIIPP (with small-employer exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers are required to prepare a Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Program (HIIPP); however, employers with 10 or fewer employees do not have to write out their HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote indicates the small-employer procedural exception (no written HIIPP required for employers with 10 or fewer employees). OSHA elsewhere discusses the proportion of establishments estimated to lack a HIIPP and assumptions about which will write from scratch versus use templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest break requirements tied to heat triggers (initial and high triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard distinguishes between an initial heat trigger (which requires if-needed rest breaks) and a high heat trigger (which requires scheduled rest breaks). Whether scheduled breaks are required depends on the duration the high heat trigger is met during a shift (e.g., a high heat trigger met for less than two hours may not trigger scheduled-break requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses numerical benchmarks in cost calculations (e.g., 47 minutes for outdoor employees, 41 minutes for indoor employees as denominators in presenting unit time cost savings) and classifies workers into groups to estimate baseline compliance and cost savings. OSHA acknowledges simplifying assumptions (e.g., assuming full 8-hour shifts at or above triggers) and requests comment on alternative methodologies. Employers should apply the trigger definitions and timing to determine when scheduled vs. if-needed breaks are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for new/returning employees' if-needed rest breaks in acclimatization costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If-needed rest breaks by new and returning employees when the temperature meets or exceeds the initial heat trigger and is below the high heat trigger are accounted for in the acclimatization costs. To avoid double counting, if-needed rest breaks were not costed for these employees during their first week of work (for new hires) or the first week back from leave (for returning workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is principally a cost-accounting and implementation guidance point: OSHA clarifies how it treats if-needed rest breaks for acclimatization in its economic analysis and how employers should expect acclimatization-related break practices to be considered for compliance/costing purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer measurement obligations (indoor) under paragraph (d)(3)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers conducting on-site measurements must follow the conditions and requirements in paragraph (d)(3)(ii) for indoor work areas (including making and retaining records as specified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule references paragraph (d)(3)(ii) for the substantive measurement obligation; recordkeeping (written/electronic, 6-month retention) is required when those measurements are conducted. OSHA cross-references these provisions rather than restating all measurement procedures in this chunk.
